item.title: From ‘May’ to ‘Is’: Certainty Distortion in Language Model Rewriting
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In From ‘May’ to ‘Is’: Certainty Distortion in Language Model Rewriting [1] (arXiv preprint, June 2026), Catarina G. Belém, Shang Wu, Hongyu Yao, Mark Steyvers, Sameer Singh, and Padhraic Smyth (UC Irvine + MIT) show that when language models paraphrase, simplify, or summarize scientific and medical text, they tend to strengthen how confidently a claim is stated even while keeping its meaning intact, turning a hedged “may” into a flat “is.”

Humans increasingly turn to Language Models (LMs) in ways that shape beliefs and drive decisions, including discussing, rewriting, and summarizing information from scientific articles, news, and medical reports. However, in these domains, where how confidently a claim is expressed matters, little is known about whether LMs faithfully preserve it. In this work, we investigate certainty distortion in LMs, defined as meaningful changes in expressed certainty when semantic content is preserved. We propose an LM-based evaluation metric that is consistent with population-level judgments of certainty. Using this metric, we characterize certainty distortion across different sizes and families of models in the context of scientific and medical communication tasks. Our results show that certainty distortion affects up to 75% of LM outputs and is systematically asymmetric in rewriting tasks with most LMs being 1.5-2× more likely to increase the expressed certainty than to decrease it. These effects can compound over repeated paraphrasing: in the medical domain, claude-haiku-4-5 increases certainty of 20% examples after a single iteration, increasing to 40% after five iterations. Prompt-based interventions reduce overall certainty distortion but do not eliminate it. Together, these findings reveal a general bias toward inflating expressed certainty, with direct implications for users who rely on LMs in high-stakes domains.

Methods

The paper defines certainty distortion (CD) as a genuine change in how confidently a claim is expressed when the meaning is held fixed, and splits it by direction: CD-↑ is inflation (the rewrite is judged more certain than the source) and CD-↓ is deflation (less certain). The hard part is measuring a subjective property at scale, since perceived certainty is a matter of human judgment rather than a fact with an answer key. The metric the paper proposes is an LM-as-judge comparison:

  • The judge () sees the original text and the rewrite, presented anonymously as Text A and Text B to avoid an order or label bias.
  • It picks which one communicates the main finding with greater certainty on a 5-point scale (Clearly A, A, No clear difference, B, Clearly B), mapped to .
  • A clear shift away from zero counts as distortion, signed for direction.

To check that the judge stands in for a reader, the authors run a human study and measure each annotator’s agreement with the population consensus (the leave-one-out mean of the other annotators) using the Kendall rank correlation. The LM judge tracks the consensus better than the average individual annotator does ( versus ), and beats a prior BERT-based certainty estimator (, a gap of in its favor). A judge that matches the human consensus more closely than individual humans match each other is a counterintuitive result, and part of it comes from how the consensus is computed rather than from the judge being genuinely better, so Figure 2 looks more favorable to the judge than a like-for-like comparison would. I come back to this in a note below.

Results

The evaluation covers two domains and four content-preserving tasks: paraphrasing, news-style rewriting, simplification, and summarization. In each case a model produces one of these rewrites from a source text, and the judge then compares its output against the original:

  • Science: SPICED [2], a dataset of single-sentence scientific findings, each paired with a news and a social-media version. The model rewrites the finding itself, either paraphrasing it or recasting it as a New York Times sentence. The paper uses the finding as the source and keeps only those whose paired news version conveys the same information, scoring at least 4 on SPICED’s information matching score (an averaged human 1-to-5 rating of whether two texts state the same finding). A new set of 500 academic abstracts across five social- and life-science disciplines adds a document-level summarization task.
  • Medicine: the Findings sections of 800 MIMIC-CXR [3] radiology reports, kept only when they contain at least one hedged sentence so there is certainty to lose, where models either paraphrase or simplify the text.

Five instruction-tuned models are tested: Gemini 3.1 (fl), GPT-5-nano, and Claude Haiku 4.5 as closed models, and Llama 3.3 (70B) and Qwen3 (8B) as open ones. Every output is scored with the validated LM-as-judge metric, and semantic-similarity checks confirm the rewrites preserve meaning.

The main findings:

  • Distortion is common. Across tasks, average CD ranges from 30.0% (GPT-5-nano) to 49.4% (Llama 3.3 70B), and the worst single setting reaches roughly 75% (Claude Haiku 4.5 at 74.8% and Gemini 3.1 at 75.3% on news rewriting).
  • The errors point one way. In four of the five models, inflation outpaces deflation. The obvious confound is where the source starts: a text already stated with high certainty has little room to be inflated (a ceiling) and a very tentative one little room to be deflated (a floor), which on its own would produce a directional skew. Splitting the results by source certainty (low, medium, high) confirms that floor/ceiling pattern, but the magnitudes stay asymmetric, with models inflating uncertain sources more often than they deflate certain ones, so the bias is not just an artifact of the starting point.
  • It builds up in medicine. When a model rewrites its own output for up to five turns, scientific text mostly settles after the first rewrite, but radiology reports keep drifting upward: Claude Haiku 4.5 inflates 20% of examples after one turn and 40% after five.
  • Scale, temperature, and prompting each help only partly.
    • Scale: larger models within a family distort somewhat less but still substantially (46.1–70% on SPICED, 19–27.4% on MIMIC). On news rewriting, distortion falls from 74.8% to 55.7% across the Claude family while the GPT family barely moves (44.3% to 46.1%).
    • Temperature: no significant effect for most models.
    • Prompting: stacking three constraints lowers paraphrase CD from 50.6% to 40.1% and news CD from 64.3% to 41.9%, but only an explicit instruction to preserve the original certainty comes close to removing the directional bias.

The ratio (column R) makes the asymmetry concrete: it is the inflation rate divided by the deflation rate (CD-↑ over CD-↓), so a value above 1 means a model strengthens certainty more often than it weakens it. Most models fall between 1.5 and 2.0, meaning they raise certainty 1.5 to 2 times as often as they lower it. Llama 3.3 is the exception, roughly even on science and actually deflating more often than it inflates on medicine (0.6), which shows the bias is a tendency across current models rather than a universal law.

My Notes

  • A different question from self-calibration: most work on LM certainty asks whether a model’s stated confidence tracks its own accuracy, the verbalized-confidence line that runs from Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know [4] through Just Ask for Calibration [5]. This paper measures something else: whether a model preserves the certainty a source chose to express when it rewrites that source’s text. A model can be well calibrated about its own answers and still strip the hedges out of someone else’s.

  • The judge’s edge over humans is partly an artifact: the validation reports the LM judge correlating with the human consensus at against for the average annotator, but the two are scored against different targets. Each human is correlated against a leave-one-out consensus, the mean of the other annotators with itself removed, while the judge, never in the pool, is correlated against the full annotator mean. The fuller mean is a lower-variance target and spares the judge the self-exclusion penalty each human pays, so both effects favor the model. The paper’s own fair comparison is its pairwise metric, judge-to-human against human-to-human consistency (Appendix B), where the judge comes out comparable rather than better.

  • The asymmetry looks like preference tuning: the paper leaves the mechanism open. One candidate is preference optimization, which rewards direct, fluent, decisive phrasing. The same pressure shows up as overconfidence in verbalized probabilities after human-feedback fine-tuning [5] and as sycophancy toward whatever looks like the more assertive answer [6]. Hedges like “may,” “could,” and “suggests” are exactly the words a preference model learns to treat as less helpful, so a meaning-preserving rewrite quietly drops them. This is a hypothesis the results are consistent with, not something the paper tests.

  • Repeated rewrites strip out uncertainty: the broken-telephone result matters most where text is rewritten repeatedly with no human reading the intermediate steps, such as retrieval-augmented summaries, agent hand-offs, and multi-hop pipelines that paraphrase a paraphrase. Earlier broken-telephone studies tracked properties like toxicity, sentiment, and length. Certainty is more consequential because dropping a hedge changes a claim’s epistemic status, turning “may be secondary to COPD” into “is attributed to COPD” [1]. In the medical setting the drift did not saturate after one pass: Claude Haiku 4.5 doubled its inflation rate from 20% to 40% over five turns.

References

  1. Belém, Catarina G., Wu, Shang, Yao, Hongyu, Steyvers, Mark, Singh, Sameer, and Smyth, Padhraic. “From ‘May’ to ‘Is’: Certainty Distortion in Language Model Rewriting.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.07951), June 6, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07951

  2. Wright, Dustin, Pei, Jiaxin, Jurgens, David, and Augenstein, Isabelle. “Modeling Information Change in Science Communication with Semantically Matched Paraphrases.” EMNLP 2022 (arXiv:2210.13001), October 24, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13001

  3. Johnson, Alistair E. W., Pollard, Tom J., Berkowitz, Seth J., Greenbaum, Nathaniel R., Lungren, Matthew P., Deng, Chih-ying, Mark, Roger G., and Horng, Steven. “MIMIC-CXR, a de-identified publicly available database of chest radiographs with free-text reports.” Scientific Data 6:317, 2019. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0322-0

  4. Kadavath, S., Conerly, T., Askell, A., et al. “Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2207.05221), July 11, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221

  5. Tian, K., Mitchell, E., Zhou, A., Sharma, A., Rafailov, R., Yao, H., Finn, C., and Manning, C. D. “Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback.” EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.14975), May 24, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14975

  6. Sharma, M., Tong, M., Korbak, T., et al. “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models.” ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.13548), October 20, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548

Related Posts

  • Just Ask for Calibration: human-feedback fine-tuning leaves models overconfident in the probabilities they state. The inflation bias here is that same overconfidence showing up when a model rewrites text rather than answers a question.
  • Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations: trains models to express calibrated uncertainty in their own words, the constructive flip side of faithfully preserving someone else’s expressed certainty.
  • SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?: asks whether a model can put its own uncertainty into words, where this paper asks whether it preserves a source’s uncertainty across a rewrite.
  • Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models: a training-side remedy aimed at the same failure, getting models to communicate uncertainty more faithfully.

item.title: PaperTrail: A Claim-Evidence Interface for Grounding Provenance in LLM-based Scholarly Q&A
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In PaperTrail [1] (CHI 2026), Anna Martin-Boyle and Harmanpreet Kaur (University of Minnesota), with Cara Leckey and Martha Brown at NASA Langley Research Center, build an interface that decomposes both an LLM’s answer and its source papers into claims and evidence, and find that showing researchers this finer-grained provenance lowered their trust in the answers without changing how much they relied on them.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in scholarly question-answering (QA) systems to help researchers synthesize vast amounts of literature. However, these systems often produce subtle errors (e.g., unsupported claims, errors of omission), and current provenance mechanisms like source citations are not granular enough for the rigorous verification that scholarly domain requires. To address this, we introduce PaperTrail, a novel interface that decomposes both LLM answers and source documents into discrete claims and evidence, mapping them to reveal supported assertions, unsupported claims, and information omitted from the source texts. We evaluated PaperTrail in a within-subjects study with 26 researchers who performed two scholarly editing tasks using PaperTrail and a baseline interface. Our results show that PaperTrail significantly lowered participants’ trust compared to the baseline. However, this increased caution did not translate to behavioral changes, as people continued to rely on LLM-generated scholarly edits to avoid a cognitively burdensome task. We discuss the value of claim-evidence matching for understanding LLM trustworthiness in scholarly settings, and present design implications for cognition-friendly communication of provenance information.

Methods

PaperTrail’s backend turns both the source papers and the LLM’s answer into matched claim-evidence pairs through a three-stage pipeline, then the frontend renders the matches so a reader can see what is supported, what is unsupported, and what the answer left out:

  • Stage 1, paper-level extraction (offline). Each source paper is preprocessed into structured claims and supporting evidence.
  • Stage 2, answer-level extraction (real-time). The LLM’s generated answer is decomposed into its own claims and evidence as it is produced.
  • Stage 3, claim-evidence matching (real-time). Similarity search retrieves the candidate paper claims relevant to the question, and an LLM aligns the answer’s claims with them, marking each supported, unsupported, or an omission, plus an overall claim-coverage indicator.

The choice of method is fixed per step at design time, judged by whether a user query is available to guide relevance, whether the step runs offline or in real time, and how much text it must process. In the evaluated system, Stage 1 extracts paper claims with an LLM and attaches their evidence by similarity, Stage 2 decomposes the answer with an LLM, and Stage 3 does claim-level retrieval: similarity search over the corpus of individual paper claims pulls the candidates relevant to the question, and an LLM then aligns the answer’s claims with them. The paper calls Stage 3 RAG, but the unit retrieved is a single claim and the LLM only selects among the candidates, so nothing is generated.

The claim-extraction backend is validated offline by scoring its extracted claims against two reference datasets: SciClaimHunt [2], the development set (precision 0.69, recall 0.62, F1 0.65), and BioClaimDetect [3], a human-annotated out-of-distribution test of whether the pipeline generalizes (precision 0.63, recall 0.88, F1 0.73). The lower precision on BioClaimDetect comes from the pipeline splitting sentences into finer atomic claims than the human annotators did, which manual inspection confirmed were valid claims rather than extraction errors.

Results

The evaluation has two parts: an offline check that the backend extracts and matches claims well enough to trust, and a within-subjects user study with 26 researchers who completed two scholarly editing tasks, once with PaperTrail and once with a baseline that offers only sentence-level source highlighting. The study tracked three primary measures and two secondary ones, then ran Spearman correlations across them:

  • Trust (primary): subjective trust in the LLM, on the validated 1–7 TXAI (Trust in Explainable AI) scale [4], asked after each task.
  • Reliance (primary): a behavioral measure of how much of the LLM’s draft survived into the final text, computed as 1 minus the normalized token-level Levenshtein edit distance [5] between the draft and the participant’s final text. A value of 1 means no edits (full reliance), lower means more rewriting.
  • Confidence (primary): subjective confidence in the edits made and in the final text, averaged over two 1–7 items.
  • Usability (secondary): the SUPR-Q usability questionnaire [6].
  • Cognitive load (secondary): the raw NASA-TLX (Task Load Index) workload score [7].

The findings, by the paper’s result sections:

  • §6.1, primary measures: trust fell, reliance and confidence held. PaperTrail significantly lowered trust in the LLM’s answers (mean 4.22 to 3.68, p = .015, d = 0.44), the intended effect of laying out unsupported claims and omissions. Reliance barely moved (0.73 vs 0.75, p = .313), and confidence held (4.27 vs 4.05, p = .525). Readers grew more skeptical without accepting any less.
  • §6.2, secondary measures: usability dropped, effort did not. Perceived usability was significantly lower with PaperTrail (5.05 to 4.48, p = .026, d = 0.52), while self-reported cognitive load was flat (4.10 vs 4.12, p = .838) and behavioral effort showed no significant change in clicks (8.26 vs 12.47, p = .137) or messages (3.67 vs 4.08, p = .438). The finer provenance felt harder to use without measurably raising workload.
  • §6.3, correlation analysis: reliance decoupled from trust. In the baseline, reliance rose with trust (r = 0.57, p < .01) and usability (r = 0.60, p < .05), so people who trusted the system more leaned on it more. With PaperTrail, that coupling vanished: reliance no longer rose with trust. The trust-behavior gap shows up here as a broken correlation. More-educated participants also reported lower confidence with PaperTrail (r = -0.41, p < .05), a sign they were more sensitive to the provenance laid out for them.
  • The authors call this a trust-behavior gap, and they surmise why. Verifying claims is slow, deliberate work, and under load people fall back on fast, automatic acceptance, so a richer provenance display can feel like understanding without prompting an actual check. The most-cited barrier in participant feedback was time: the roughly 20-minute task plus slow system latency left no room to verify, and several participants said the time pressure made them lean on the LLM more rather than less. The authors’ reframe is from measuring trust to measuring trustworthiness, with claim-evidence matching offered as one such signal.

My Notes

  • The trust-behavior gap is partly the tool’s fault. It is also bad news for provenance-as-fix in general: a large literature assumes better explanations or citations will calibrate reliance, but here a strictly more informative display made people more skeptical without changing what they did. Some of that is human (automation bias under time pressure), but some is the design: PaperTrail flags which claims are unsupported or omitted without coupling those flags to a cheaper next action, no suggested fix, no prioritized list of what to check first, no one-click correction, so noticing a problem and resolving it still cost the reader the same. The authors half-concede this, proposing two fixes: adaptive provenance that adjusts detail by context, and progressive engagement that trains verification skill over time.

  • PaperTrail catches the two errors the companion schema paper flags most. Those are unsupported claims and omissions. That paper [8] catalogs how scholarly-QA answers go wrong, and PaperTrail decomposes both the answer and its sources into claims to flag exactly those. The two were released together but neither cites the other, so the pairing is mine: one names the failure modes, the other is built to catch them.

  • PaperTrail reuses ExpertQA’s grading primitive for reading. ExpertQA [9] split answers into claims paired with evidence so experts could grade attribution after the fact. PaperTrail runs the same decomposition in real time and puts it in front of the reader. The same claim-evidence unit works for both scoring and reading LLM answers, not just for benchmarking.

  • Omissions are what a citation checker misses. Source-citation tools verify that what was said is supported. PaperTrail also flags what the source contained but the answer dropped, the same recall-side failure that rubric-coverage benchmarks [10] measure. Putting omission detection in a live editing interface is the novel move, since omission is precisely the error a reader cannot catch by checking the citations that are present.

References

  1. Martin-Boyle, A., Leckey, C. A. C., Brown, M. C., Kaur, H.. “PaperTrail: A Claim-Evidence Interface for Grounding Provenance in LLM-based Scholarly Q&A.” CHI 2026 (arXiv:2602.21045), February 24, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21045
  2. Kumar, S., Sharma, A., Khincha, S. H., Shroff, G., Singh, S. R., Mishra, R. “SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-Based Scientific Claim Verification.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2502.10003), February 14, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10003
  3. Achakulvisut, T., Bhagavatula, C., Acuna, D., Kording, K. “Claim Extraction in Biomedical Publications using Deep Discourse Model and Transfer Learning.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:1907.00962), July 1, 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.00962
  4. Hoffman, R. R., Mueller, S. T., Klein, G., Litman, J. “Measures for Explainable AI: Explanation Goodness, User Satisfaction, Mental Models, Curiosity, Trust, and Human-AI Performance.” Frontiers in Computer Science 5, 2023. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomp.2023.1096257
  5. Levenshtein, V. I. “Binary Codes Capable of Correcting Deletions, Insertions, and Reversals.” Soviet Physics Doklady 10 (8), 1966.
  6. Sauro, J. “SUPR-Q: A Comprehensive Measure of the Quality of the Website User Experience.” Journal of Usability Studies 10 (2), 2015.
  7. Hart, S. G., Staveland, L. E. “Development of NASA-TLX (Task Load Index): Results of Empirical and Theoretical Research.” Advances in Psychology 52, 1988. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0166-4115(08)62386-9
  8. Martin-Boyle, A., Humphreys, W., Brown, M., Leckey, C., Kaur, H.. “An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems.” CHI 2026 (arXiv:2602.21059), February 24, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21059
  9. Malaviya, C., Lee, S., Chen, S., Sieber, E., Yatskar, M., Roth, D.. “ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers.” NAACL 2024 (arXiv:2309.07852), September 14, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07852
  10. Li S. Yifei, Allen Chang, Malaviya, C., Yatskar, M.. “ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2509.00496), August 30, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00496

Related Posts

  • ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers: the benchmark that established claim-evidence decomposition for grading attribution, the primitive PaperTrail moves into a live interface.
  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: a complementary approach that removes unsupported claims automatically rather than surfacing them for a human to judge.
  • AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 Queries: another high-stakes domain where unsupported claims slip past readers who only check the citations that are present.

item.title: Zen and the Art of AI Research
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Jack Morris, writing on his Substack Token for Token, lays out what becoming an AI researcher actually takes, and argues temperament matters more than talent. The piece is structured as a set of Zen koans, and its most useful advice is about how to treat your own experiments:

Did it go well? Great! Did it go poorly? Also great! Both outcomes teach you the same amount of information.

What the essay argues:

  • Reading and building, together: you become a researcher by combining reading with building, not either alone. Insights arrive at random, so most of the job is showing up with discipline, and it is possible to read too many papers rather than attempting a solution first.

  • Depth matters more than the topic: the exact problem isn’t that important, but avoid whatever has been popular for under six months. Go deep on the fundamentals that don’t change (cross-entropy, singular value decomposition, policy gradients), and avoid projects whose best outcome is a higher score on an existing benchmark.

  • Beginner’s mind: experience can work against good research intuition, since methods tuned to small scales often fail at scale. The field is young enough that no one has a long head start, so stay open and keep ego out of it.

  • Inspiration comes from away from the desk: breakthroughs often arrive unexpectedly, like the benzene ring seen in a dream or the drug Ozempic traced to lizard venom. Doing good research means doing things other than research, especially walking.

  • Experimental equanimity: a result that goes well and one that goes poorly teach you the same amount. Be most skeptical of good results, since many come from a bug rather than a real effect.

  • Don’t compare yourself to others: research is outcome-driven and peer review is neither consistent nor fair. The useful question when you admire a result is whether you were working at the depth to have found it yourself.

  • Most of the work is gruntwork: ambitious projects involve hundreds of unglamorous hours, like hand-labeling data or filtering datasets by hand. Time spent in obscurity is normal, and the difficulty is a feature rather than a bug.

  • Healthy paranoia about bugs: many ideas fail not because they are wrong but because of an unfound bug in a complex stack. If a metric looks off you cannot move on, so log everything and chase down why.

  • Fast iteration over parallelism: experiments take too long and context switching is costly, so design workflows for fast experimental feedback. Some results still take an unavoidably long time, and maintaining state across days is its own skill.

  • Coding agents make two problems worse: they make it easier to lose track of details and to context-switch, and an agent can quietly change a config or shorten a run. Small engineering slips are scientifically grave, so you still have to understand the system that produced your results.

  • Temperament over talent: the closing claim is that persistence, curiosity, and meticulousness matter more than raw ability.

My Notes

  • The same temperament running teaches: if you remove the AI specifics, this post sounds almost like advice for training for endurance-sport: show up even on bad days, treat a good result and a bad one as equally informative, distrust anything that looks too good, and accept that most of the work is grunt work. I have learned much from running as well as from research!

Related Posts

  • Proof Generation vs Digestion: Tao’s warning that AI races through proof generation and verification while leaving understanding behind, the same gap this essay names for research code.
  • Journey into Coding with AI [2/4]: Shifting Gears: on how much control to cede to coding AI and what judgment stays human, the tension the essay’s last sections work through.
  • NLP Benchmark Saturation: why benchmark-chasing has diminishing returns, the structural backdrop to the essay’s “don’t chase benchmarks.”
  • “Skills” Are Not Software Engineering: keeping engineering rigor rather than outsourcing it wholesale, a parallel to refusing to outsource understanding.
  • Terence Tao’s ChatGPT Research Buddy: Tao using ChatGPT as a research aid while keeping control of the math, the productive counterpart to the essay’s caution about not outsourcing understanding.

item.title: Harness Engineering
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Ryan Lopopolo, writing for OpenAI, reports on an experiment in Harness Engineering: Leveraging Codex in an Agent-First World: over five months a small team shipped an internal product of roughly a million lines of code with zero manually-written lines, every line produced by Codex while humans steered.

What the article reports:

  • Starting from an empty repository: the first commit landed in late August 2025, and Codex generated the initial scaffold, including the AGENTS.md that tells agents how to work there. Over five months it grew to roughly a million lines across about 1,500 merged pull requests, with the team going from three engineers to seven at around 3.5 PRs per engineer per day. The core rule held throughout: no manually-written code.

  • Redefining the engineer’s role: early progress was slow not because Codex was incapable but because the environment was underspecified, so the job became enabling the agent. Work went depth-first, and when something failed the question was “what capability is missing, and how do we make it both legible and enforceable for the agent?” Humans interact almost entirely through prompts, and review was pushed agent-to-agent, with Codex reviewing its own changes and requesting further agent reviews in a loop until the reviewers are satisfied.

  • Making the application legible: as throughput rose, human QA capacity became the bottleneck, so the team exposed the running app to Codex. The app is bootable per git worktree, the Chrome DevTools Protocol is wired into the agent runtime, and logs and metrics are queryable via LogQL and PromQL. Prompts like “ensure service startup completes in under 800ms” become checkable, and single runs work a task for six hours or more, often overnight.

  • Repository knowledge as the system of record: one big AGENTS.md failed, since it crowded out the task, rotted into stale rules, and resisted mechanical checks. It became a roughly 100-line table of contents pointing into a structured docs/ tree of design docs, plans, and references. Plans are first-class versioned artifacts, the layout supports progressive disclosure, and linters plus a recurring “doc-gardening” agent keep it current.

  • Agent legibility as the goal: the repository is optimized first for what Codex can read, on the principle that “anything it can’t access in-context while running effectively doesn’t exist,” so knowledge in Slack, Google Docs, or people’s heads has to be pushed into the repo. They favored “boring,” composable technologies the agent can model, and sometimes reimplemented a subset of a library, such as their own concurrency helper instead of a generic package, rather than wrap opaque upstream behavior.

  • Enforcing invariants, not implementations: a rigid layered architecture (Types → Config → Repo → Service → Runtime → UI, with cross-cutting concerns entering through Providers) is enforced mechanically by custom, agent-written linters and structural tests, alongside “taste invariants” like structured logging and file-size limits. The principle is to enforce boundaries centrally and allow autonomy locally, and output that doesn’t match human style is fine as long as it stays correct, maintainable, and legible to the next agent run.

  • Throughput changes the merge philosophy: with agent output far exceeding human attention, the repository runs with minimal blocking merge gates, short-lived pull requests, and test flakes handled by follow-up runs rather than blocking. Corrections are cheap and waiting is expensive, a tradeoff they call irresponsible at low throughput and often correct here.

  • What “agent-generated” covers: everything, including product code and tests, CI and release tooling, internal developer tools, documentation, evaluation harnesses, review comments, repository-management scripts, and dashboard definitions. Humans stay in the loop at a higher layer, prioritizing work, translating user feedback into acceptance criteria, and validating outcomes.

  • Crossing into end-to-end autonomy: from a single prompt, Codex can now validate the codebase, reproduce a reported bug, record a video of the failure, implement and validate a fix, record a second video, open a pull request, respond to feedback, remediate build failures, escalate only when judgment is required, and merge. The report cautions this depends on the repository’s specific structure and tooling and should not be assumed to generalize without similar investment.

  • Entropy and garbage collection: full autonomy means Codex replicates existing patterns, including the bad ones, so the codebase drifts. The team used to spend a fifth of every week hand-cleaning “AI slop,” then replaced that with encoded “golden principles” and recurring cleanup agents that scan for deviations and open small refactors, treating technical debt like a high-interest loan paid down continuously.

  • What they are still unsure of: the approach has held through internal launch and adoption, but they don’t yet know how architectural coherence evolves over years in a fully agent-generated system, where human judgment matters most, or how it changes as models improve. Their summary is that the discipline now shows up in the environment and feedback loops more than in the code.

My Notes

  • Two views of the same problem: this report and a source-level read of Anthropic’s Claude Code, Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems, emphasize different halves of the same system. OpenAI’s account is mostly about the environment the agent works in (the repository as system of record, enforced layering, agent-to-agent review), and the Claude Code read is mostly about the agent program itself (a single agent loop, the permission system, the tools it exposes). Where they meet is the bet that the real engineering lives in the structure around the model rather than the model itself, which is also why the Claude Code analysis finds the loop nearly trivial and almost all the code in the systems wrapped around it.

  • The scarce resource is human attention: the entire design treats human time and attention as the fixed constraint and reorganizes everything else around it. Legible logs, progressive-disclosure docs, a map instead of a manual: these are all ways to spend less human attention per unit of agent work. It’s the same context-engineering discipline the field has been converging on, here applied at repository scale, and it generalizes past coding to any agentic pipeline. The move from a retrieval flow to a navigable repository the agent investigates on its own is the same reframing as Filesystems vs. RAG.

  • The engineers moved up a layer: the headline (a million lines, zero hand-written, a tenth of the time) is the part everyone repeats, but the report is careful that the end-to-end autonomy “depends heavily on the specific structure and tooling of this repository and should not be assumed to generalize without similar investment.” Humans went from writing code to specifying intent, encoding invariants, and validating outcomes, which is the same division of labor argued in “Skills” Are Not Software Engineering: the model proposes, and a deterministic layer of linters and structural tests enforces correctness.

  • Constraints enable the speed: the team front-loaded the kind of rigid architecture you normally postpone until you have hundreds of engineers, because for agents the constraints are what allow speed without decay. The operational detail worth stealing is that the custom lint error messages are written to inject remediation instructions into the agent’s context. In a human workflow these rules would feel pedantic. With agents, once encoded they apply everywhere at once.

  • Autonomous generation produces entropy: Codex replicates whatever patterns already exist, including the bad ones, so the codebase drifts. The team spent a fifth of every week hand-cleaning “AI slop” until that obviously didn’t scale, then replaced it with encoded “golden principles” and recurring cleanup agents. A million lines in five months is also a million lines no human has read line by line, and the bet is that agent-legibility plus tests substitute for that reading. Whether that holds over years is exactly what the report says it doesn’t yet know, the same gap between production and understanding that Proof Generation vs Digestion names for mathematics.

Related Posts

  • Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems: a source-level read of how a coding agent is actually architected, the design-space view this report’s practices fit into.
  • “Skills” Are Not Software Engineering: the model-proposes, runtime-ensures-correctness split that the enforced invariants and linters here implement.
  • Filesystems vs. RAG: repository-as-context and “give Codex a map,” the same reframing the report’s knowledge base makes.
  • Proof Generation vs Digestion: production outrunning understanding, the open question behind a million unread lines.

item.title: An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems [1] (CHI 2026), Anna Martin-Boyle and Harmanpreet Kaur (University of Minnesota), with William Humphreys, Martha Brown, and Cara Leckey at NASA Langley Research Center, build a schema of how working scientists actually judge LLM answers about their own field, arguing that automated metrics miss how they assess those answers.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming scholarly tasks like search and summarization, but their reliability remains uncertain. Current evaluation metrics for testing LLM reliability are primarily automated approaches that prioritize efficiency and scalability, but lack contextual nuance and fail to reflect how scientific domain experts assess LLM outputs in practice. We developed and validated a schema for evaluating LLM errors in scholarly question-answering systems that reflects the assessment strategies of practicing scientists. In collaboration with domain experts, we identified 20 error patterns across seven categories through thematic analysis of 68 question-answer pairs. We validated this schema through contextual inquiries with 10 additional scientists, which showed not only which errors experts naturally identify but also how structured evaluation schemas can help them detect previously overlooked issues. Domain experts use systematic assessment strategies, including technical precision testing, value-based evaluation, and meta-evaluation of their own practices. We discuss implications for supporting expert evaluation of LLM outputs, including opportunities for personalized, schema-driven tools that adapt to individual evaluation patterns and expertise levels.

Methods

The study runs a retrieval-augmented QA system over scientific papers (documents are chunked, vectorized, retrieved per question, and fed to an LLM that generates a long-form answer), then examines how domain experts evaluate its output in two phases. The LLM-generated answers are the object of evaluation throughout, and the two phases use different sets of them: the Phase 1 answers became the coded data that built the schema, while in Phase 2 a fresh batch was the material experts evaluated to validate it.

  • Phase 1, schema development. Three NASA Langley scientists took part. Two posed questions about papers they had authored (28 in aeroacoustics, 40 in non-destructive evaluation) and the QA system generated an LLM answer to each, so the ground truth was known to the evaluator. The third wrote no questions and was kept aside to label those answers for errors independently, a perspective the authors kept unbiased by not having that expert author any of the questions. Thematic analysis of the resulting 68 question-answer pairs yielded 20 recurring error patterns, organized into seven categories. The complete schema is in The Schema below.
  • Phase 2, schema validation. Ten additional scientists each wrote questions about their own papers, and the system generated LLM answers that the experts evaluated in think-aloud contextual inquiries. They evaluated unaided first, then with the schema (the Phase 1 list of 20 error patterns grouped into seven categories) in hand, to test whether it helped them catch errors they had missed.

Across both phases the authors collected 188 expert-posed questions and sorted them into 11 question types (a separate classification from the error schema, grouping the questions rather than the errors):

  • Methodological Inquiry and Improvement: compares approaches and asks how methods could be transferred or refined.
  • Meta-Analysis and Contextualization: asks about institutional motivations and synthesizes insights across multiple papers.
  • Critical Evaluation and Validation: probes assumptions and biases, and whether research choices were adequately justified.
  • Application and Practical Implications: asks how findings translate to real-world use and what tradeoffs implementation brings.
  • Technical Details and Specifications: asks for the parameters, equations, or configurations needed to replicate the work.
  • Definitions and Concepts: asks to clarify core ideas and key terms.
  • Future Directions and Extrapolation: looks past current findings to next steps and where the research is heading.
  • Binary / Factual Verification: asks to confirm or deny a discrete fact, without interpretation.
  • External Context: asks for knowledge beyond the paper, such as external standards or developments since publication.
  • Numerical Analysis and Derivation: asks the system to calculate or reason mathematically with data from the paper.
  • Procedural Information: asks how a study was conducted, focusing on the sequence of steps.

They then mapped the error patterns against each question type (Figure 2, the cover heatmap).

The Schema

The full taxonomy, for reference: 20 error patterns under seven categories, paraphrased from the paper’s Tables 1 and 2 [1]. Hallucinations are a single pattern broken out into seven sub-types.

  • Incorrect answer
    • Completely incorrect: the answer is entirely wrong.
    • Partially incorrect: a mix of right and wrong, covering basic accuracy slips, misinterpreting paper content, self-contradiction, reference confusion, and misread tables or equations.
    • Superfluous content: irrelevant or unnecessary information.
  • Hallucinations (plausible-looking content that is fabricated or false)
    • Terminology: invented or wrongly defined terms and acronyms.
    • Numerical data: made-up statistics, measurements, or metrics.
    • Mathematical constructs: invented equations, formulae, or relationships.
    • Technical content: false technical characteristics, properties, limitations, or capabilities.
    • External context and world knowledge: wrong general science or related-literature claims.
    • Document structure: invented page, section, table, or figure numbers.
    • Citation information: fabricated citations or parts of them (authors, dates, titles, venues, DOIs, page numbers).
  • Incomplete answer
    • Major omissions: important content left out: an ignored section, a missed main point, an ignored paper in a multi-document question, an incomplete definition, missing references, or chronological gaps.
    • Lacking details: high-level concepts present but lower-level detail missing.
    • Multimedia comprehension: fails to connect formats, for example not linking a table to its caption or in-text reference.
  • Question interpretation
    • Question misinterpretation: a wrong reading that leads to a wrong answer.
    • Question redirection: answers a different question than the one asked.
  • Synthesis issues
    • Document linking failure: can’t tie information to the right document across multiple papers.
    • Chronological confusion: misreads temporal relationships.
    • Disjointed response: fragmented or poorly integrated, for example discussing each paper in isolation.
    • Source confusion: misattributes information across papers.
  • Formatting issues
    • Verbosity: unnecessarily wordy or repetitive.
    • Notation errors: incorrect technical notation.
    • Language issues: improper wording, spelling, grammar, or syntax.
    • Inconsistent referencing: inconsistent in how it references content.
  • System failures
    • LLM limitations: model-inherent issues such as limited context length, no multi-modal understanding, and no access to external libraries.
    • Retrieval failures: the retriever did not supply the needed context.
    • Data structure issues: internal data-organization problems leaking into outputs.

Results

Because this is a qualitative HCI study rather than a leaderboard, the results are the schema itself and the evaluation behavior it exposes, validated through the two-phase design (3 experts in development, 10 in validation, all recruited through NASA Langley’s internal networks).

  • The schema generalizes to a second expert group. All seven categories reappeared in Phase 2’s independent coding of the 10 new experts’ unprompted feedback, which suggests expert error-spotting is consistent across people rather than an artifact of the development team.
  • Experts evaluate with structured strategies, not gut reaction. They apply technical precision testing, value-based assessment tied to research use, and meta-evaluation of their own checking process, behavior that automated metrics do not model.
  • The schema is also a scaffold. Giving experts the schema during contextual inquiries turned up errors they had overlooked when evaluating unaided. The most common were hallucinated or misattributed citations, but experts also caught missing tables and figures, chronological gaps, disjointed responses, and missed main points once the inventory prompted them to look. The taxonomy does double duty as a checklist for human review.
  • Error profiles differ by question type (Figure 2). The 11 question types do not fail the same way, which suggests evaluation and mitigation should be differentiated by question type rather than applied uniformly.

My Notes

  • This is the human-process complement to the automated-benchmark line, and it is openly skeptical of it. Benchmarks like ExpertQA [2] and ResearchQA [3] push toward scalable automated scoring, while this paper argues those metrics are too coarse to capture how experts judge, and studies the assessment process itself. The two programs answer different questions, what a good answer should contain versus how a scientist decides whether it does, and the schema is the missing description of the second.

  • Evaluators grading answers about their own papers provides strong but narrow ground truth. Recruiting scientists to assess QA output on work they authored removes the usual annotator-knowledge gap, since they know what the correct answer is. The cost is scale and breadth: 3 experts in development and 10 in validation, all from one research center, which makes the schema’s categories credible but their relative frequencies hard to generalize.

  • The schema-as-scaffold result is the practically useful finding. That structured prompts help experts catch overlooked errors matches a long line of checklist research in medicine and aviation, where externalizing tacit criteria improves detection. It points at the paper’s own proposed direction: schema-driven review tools.

  • Error-by-question-type echoes the cross-benchmark pattern that difficulty is not uniform. ExpertQA found list, advice, and opinion questions hardest [2], and this paper independently finds error profiles vary by question type. The convergence across an automated benchmark and a qualitative study is the stronger signal: question type, not just domain, is a primary driver of LLM-QA difficulty.

References

  1. Martin-Boyle, A., Humphreys, W., Brown, M., Leckey, C., Kaur, H.. “An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems.” CHI 2026 (arXiv:2602.21059), February 24, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21059
  2. Malaviya, C., Lee, S., Chen, S., Sieber, E., Yatskar, M., Roth, D.. “ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers.” NAACL 2024 (arXiv:2309.07852), September 14, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07852
  3. Li S. Yifei, Allen Chang, Malaviya, C., Yatskar, M.. “ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2509.00496), August 30, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00496

Related Posts

  • ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers: the automated benchmark this study implicitly critiques, and the source of the matching question-type-difficulty finding.
  • TruthfulQA: Are Larger LLMs More Truthful?: an early factuality benchmark whose single-metric framing this paper argues is too coarse for how experts actually judge answers.
  • AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 Queries: another domain (law) where expert-grounded error analysis exposes failures automated scoring understates.

item.title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Automated Design of Agentic Systems [1] (ICLR 2025), Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, and Jeff Clune at the University of British Columbia and the Vector Institute argue that the design of LLM-powered agents should itself be automated, and introduce Meta Agent Search as a first instance.

Researchers are investing substantial effort in developing powerful general-purpose agents, wherein Foundation Models are used as modules within agentic systems (e.g. Chain-of-Thought, Self-Reflection, Toolformer). However, the history of machine learning teaches us that hand-designed solutions are eventually replaced by learned solutions. We describe a newly forming research area, Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS), which aims to automatically create powerful agentic system designs, including inventing novel building blocks and/or combining them in new ways. We further demonstrate that there is an unexplored yet promising approach within ADAS where agents can be defined in code and new agents can be automatically discovered by a meta agent programming ever better ones in code. Given that most programming languages are Turing Complete, this approach theoretically enables the learning of any possible agentic system: including novel prompts, tool use, workflows, and combinations thereof. We present a simple yet effective algorithm named Meta Agent Search to demonstrate this idea, where a meta agent iteratively programs interesting new agents based on an ever-growing archive of previous discoveries. Through extensive experiments across multiple domains including coding, science, and math, we show that our algorithm can progressively invent agents with novel designs that greatly outperform state-of-the-art hand-designed agents. Importantly, we consistently observe the surprising result that agents invented by Meta Agent Search maintain superior performance even when transferred across domains and models, demonstrating their robustness and generality. Provided we develop it safely, our work illustrates the potential of an exciting new research direction toward automatically designing ever-more powerful agentic systems to benefit humanity.

Methods

The authors cast Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS) as an optimization problem with three components (Figure 2):

  • Search space: the set of agent designs the method can represent. Meta Agent Search makes this Python code: an agent is a forward(task) function that may call foundation-model APIs, use tools, keep internal state, and compose sub-agents. Because the language is Turing-complete, the space in principle covers any prompt, tool-use pattern, or workflow, not just variations on a fixed template.
  • Search algorithm: how the space is explored. A meta agent (a frontier LLM, GPT-4 in the experiments) reads an archive of previously discovered agents and programs a new one.
  • Evaluation function: how a candidate is scored. Each new agent runs on a held-out validation split of the target task, and its accuracy or F1 is the signal the meta agent maximizes.

The search loop is short. The meta agent works against a roughly 100-line framework that supplies basic primitives like foundation-model queries and prompt formatting, so it only writes the forward function, the same trick FunSearch [2] used to evolve programs from a small set of given building blocks. Each iteration runs four steps:

  • The archive is optionally seeded with baseline agents such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Refine.
  • Conditioned on the whole archive, the meta agent writes a high-level description of a new agent (the prompt asks for one that is “interestingly new”) and then its code, with two self-reflection passes meant to keep the design novel.
  • The candidate runs on validation data. If it errors, the meta agent revises the code, repeating up to five times.
  • The working agent and its score are appended to the archive, and the next iteration conditions on the larger archive.

The archive is the memory that lets each iteration build on the last. Because it stores each agent’s full source code, not just a description, a new agent can copy and recombine code from earlier ones rather than start from scratch. The paper shows several designs discovered on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) reusing earlier “stepping stones”: a multi-chain-of-thought-then-ensemble pattern that first appeared at iteration 3, and expert-critic ideas from iterations 5, 11, and 12 that the best agent later combined.

Results

The experiments span three settings, all run with the same algorithm and only task-specific prompt text changed. The ARC abstraction benchmark is the case study. Four benchmarks covering reading, math, science, and multi-task reasoning (DROP, MGSM, MMLU, GPQA) are the main comparison. Held-out tasks and swapped base models test transfer. In every setting the meta agent is GPT-4, while the discovered agents and all baselines are scored with the cheaper GPT-3.5 over five runs each, reporting median accuracy or F1 with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval. The baselines are the standard hand-designed scaffolds (Chain-of-Thought, self-consistency, Self-Refine, LLM-Debate, Quality-Diversity, Step-back Abstraction, Role Assignment) plus the prompt-optimization method OPRO [3] , so the comparison isolates what searching over code buys beyond searching over prompts.

The ARC case study shows the search dynamic most clearly. Over 25 iterations, held-out test accuracy climbs from about 6% to 14%, above every hand-designed baseline. The left panel of Figure 3 tracks that climb and marks the iterations where key ideas first appeared. The right panel shows the best agent found, a “Structured Feedback and Ensemble” design that generates five chains of thought, routes them through three expert critics (efficiency, readability, simplicity) plus a human-like critic, and ensembles three refinement passes.

Across the four reasoning benchmarks the same ranking holds, and the margins are largest exactly where the base model already has the knowledge but makes avoidable errors:

  • Reading comprehension (DROP): 79.4 F1 against 65.8 for the best hand-designed agent, a 13.6-point gain.
  • Math (MGSM): 53.4% against 39.0% for LLM-Debate, the best baseline, a 14.4-point gain.
  • Multi-task (MMLU) and science (GPQA): smaller margins (69.6% vs. 67.6%, 34.6% vs. 32.9%), which the authors attribute to the base model lacking the underlying knowledge rather than the scaffold failing.
  • Cross-domain transfer: the top-3 agents found on MGSM, moved to held-out GSM8K and GSM-Hard, add 25.9% and 13.2% over the baselines. Moved to non-math MMLU and DROP they still beat the hand-designed scaffolds.
  • Cross-model transfer: the top-3 ARC agents found with GPT-3.5 keep their lead when run on Claude Haiku, GPT-4, and Claude Sonnet, with Sonnet reaching nearly 50% on ARC.

Meta Agent Search wins every column of the head-to-head, and it beats OPRO in all four domains, the result the authors lean on to argue that searching over whole agents, not just prompts, is what pays off.

My Notes

  • Transfer is the result that matters, and it comes from the scaffolds being domain-agnostic: it outweighs the ARC gain, a large relative jump on small absolute numbers (human-level is around 80% [4]). Scaffolds discovered on one task keep working on different tasks and on different base models, because the designs are reasoning-and-control patterns that manipulate model calls without encoding the task itself, with the task-specific content kept in the prompt the agent receives rather than in its code, so they behave less like solvers tuned to one benchmark. This parallels Promptbreeder [5], where evolved prompts transferred, but here the unit that transfers is executable code, a broader portability claim. The search optimized accuracy on a single domain with no cross-domain objective, yet the agents transfer anyway, which is good held-out evidence that the generality is real rather than fit to one benchmark. Optimizing for it directly is still untried.
  • Code as the search space: earlier automated-prompting work (OPRO [3], APE [6], Promptbreeder) searches over strings fed to a fixed scaffold, and DSPy [7] compiles a human-written module graph, optimizing the prompts and demonstrations inside it rather than the graph itself. ADAS widens the space to code, so the meta agent can invent new control flow (loops, early-exit, ensembles, self-critique), not just better prompts inside an existing shape. AFlow [8] , published around the same time, makes a different trade: it searches a graph over a fixed library of operators with Monte Carlo tree search. ADAS and AFlow leave open whether to search over open-ended code or a fixed operator graph.
  • The archive both enables the search and makes it expensive: Meta Agent Search is a novelty-seeking search with an LLM as the mutation operator, and the archive of past designs lets each round build on earlier ones. That same archive makes each step expensive: 25 iterations on ARC and 30 on the reasoning benchmarks, each generating one candidate, running two self-reflection passes, and allowing up to five error-driven refinements, with every accepted candidate scored on the full validation set. Scaling to harder benchmarks runs into the sample-efficiency limit that prompt-optimization methods like OPRO [3] also hit, and surrogate scoring to avoid running every candidate on the full eval set is the obvious follow-up.
  • On the intrinsic-to-extrinsic spectrum of self-improving agents: that spectrum [9], from Liu and van der Schaar, runs from agents that set their own learning loop (intrinsic) to loops fully fixed by humans (extrinsic). ADAS is more intrinsic than the earlier prompt-search optimizers: the meta agent reasons over the archive in an open-ended code space to decide what to build next, which is autonomous metacognitive planning rather than algorithmic mutation, and code can in principle express agents that improve themselves. But the parts that decide what counts as better stay human-fixed: the objective (validation accuracy on a chosen benchmark), the evaluation function, the archive mechanism, the stopping point. So it is a mixed case, not the fully extrinsic end: autonomous proposal inside a human-designed objective and loop. The paper’s own thesis, that hand-designed solutions are eventually replaced by learned ones, applies to the agents but not yet to the loop that finds them. Making that loop learned, a self-referential meta agent that improves itself, is the direction the authors flag as future work. The same team took that step in the Darwin Gödel Machine [10] , where agents rewrite their own code against a growing archive of variants.
  • The “provided we develop it safely” caveat points at a real property of the method: the abstract’s closing line is not boilerplate. A loop that proposes and executes arbitrary code is a capability-elicitation concern once it is pointed at an open-ended objective rather than a sandboxed benchmark, closer in shape to AutoGPT-style self-improvement than to prompt search. Clune’s earlier argument for AI-generating algorithms [11] is the right context for reading the paper’s scope.

References

  2. Romera-Paredes, B., Barekatain, M., Novikov, A., Balog, M., Kumar, M. P., Dupont, E., Ruiz, F. J. R., Ellenberg, J.   • EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers: the same LLM-as-mutation-operator pattern over a narrower, prompt-only search space.
